result: Homeostatic synaptic plasticity is impaired in Rab3a−/− and Rab3a Earlybird mutant cortical cultures. TTX treatment increased mEPSC amplitude in wild-type cultures (13.9 ± 0.7 to 18.2 ± 0.9 pA), but not in Rab3a−/− cultures (13.6 ± 0.1 vs. 14.3 ± 0.6 pA) or Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures (15.1 ± 1.0 vs. 14.6 ± 1.1 pA).
evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this as the major finding of the study. Reviewer 1 states 'The major finding - impaired homeostatic up-scaling after TTX treatment in Rab3A KO and Rab3 earlybird mutant neurons - is supported by data of high quality.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The authors clearly demonstrate the Rab3A plays a role in HSP at excitatory synapses, with substantially less plasticity occurring in the Rab3A KO neurons.'

result: Baseline mEPSC amplitude is elevated in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures compared to wild-type (15.1 ± 1.0 pA vs. 11.0 ± 0.7 pA, p = 0.04), consistent with findings at the NMJ.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges this finding, noting 'There is also no apparent HSP in the Earlybird Rab3A mutation, although baseline synaptic strength is already elevated.' The reviewers discuss this as potentially representing occlusion but do not challenge the data itself.

result: The TTX-induced increase in mEPSC amplitude does not depend on Ca2+-permeable receptors, as NASPM application did not reverse the TTX effect on amplitude (before NASPM: CON 12.9 ± 3.5 pA, TTX 17.5 ± 3.1 pA; after NASPM: CON 11.9 ± 2.6 pA, TTX 16.1 ± 3.5 pA).
evaluation: Reviewer 3 challenges this interpretation, noting 'the amplitude data show a strong trend towards smaller amplitude following NASPM treatment (Fig 3B). The p value for both control and TTX neurons was 0.08 - it is very difficult to argue that there is no effect.' The reviewer suggests heterogeneity in receptor composition may complicate the interpretation.

result: NASPM reduced mEPSC frequency, with a greater reduction after TTX treatment, suggesting activity blockade promotes synaptic sites containing only Ca2+-permeable receptors that do not contribute to amplitude increases.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the interpretation, stating 'there is a strong frequency effect that is unclear in origin' and suggests alternative explanations including 'pre-synaptic NASPM-sensitive receptors that influence release probability.' The mechanism remains unclear despite the data.

result: GluA2 receptor cluster size showed a trend toward increase after TTX (18.1%) similar in magnitude to mEPSC amplitude increase (19.7%), but did not reach statistical significance. No trend was observed in Rab3a−/− cultures.
evaluation: Multiple reviewers identify this as a critical weakness. Reviewer 1 states 'The data on GluA2 modulation after TTX incubation are likely statistically underpowered and do not allow drawing solid conclusions, such as GluA2-independent mechanisms of up-scaling.' Reviewer 2 questions whether 'it is impossible to determine if Rab3A is involved at all' and notes this 'question has not been answered.' Reviewer 3 states 'it remains difficult to distinguish if the apparent difference in imaging and electrophysiology is a methodological issue rather than a biological one.'

result: VGLUT1 immunofluorescence was not increased after activity blockade in wild-type or Rab3a−/− cultures, providing no evidence for increased glutamate transporter levels contributing to homeostatic plasticity.
evaluation: This negative result is not challenged by reviewers and is consistent with previous literature cited by the authors. The finding is accepted as ruling out one potential presynaptic mechanism.

result: Rab3a acts in neurons rather than glia. mEPSC amplitudes increased when Rab3a was present in neurons (WT on WT: CON 13.3 ± 0.5 pA, TTX 16.7 ± 1.2 pA; WT on KO: CON 13.3 ± 1.0 pA, TTX 18.8 ± 1.4 pA), but not when present only in glia (KO on WT: CON 15.2 ± 1.1 pA, TTX 16.9 ± 0.7 pA).
evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The authors have solid data showing that Rab3A is unlikely to be active in astrocytes.' However, Reviewer 3 also notes 'The section on TNF is a bit odd. The data on the astrocyte deletion of Rab3A only argues that Rab3A is unlikely to regulate TNF release. But it could easily be downstream of the neuronal TNF receptor.'

result: Loss of Rab3a in glia did not disrupt homeostatic plasticity, suggesting Rab3a-dependent homeostatic increase is unlikely via the astrocytic-TNFα pathway, and may involve a non-TNFα mechanism.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly challenges this interpretation: 'The section on TNF is a bit odd. The data on the astrocyte deletion of Rab3A only argues that Rab3A is unlikely to regulate TNF release. But it could easily be downstream of the neuronal TNF receptor. Without any data addressing the TNF response, it seems quite premature to argue that Rab3A is part of a TNF-independent pathway.'

result: This is the first demonstration that a protein thought to function presynaptically is required for homeostatic synaptic plasticity of quantal size in central neurons.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges this claim: 'The section title (line 506-7) declaring Rab3A as the first presynaptic protein involved in HSP is also premature, as they don't know it is acting pre-synaptically.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'acknowledge that they should restrict their conclusions to the data in the current study' and questions whether interpretations about presynaptic action should be in the abstract.

result: The lack of robust increase in receptor levels leaves open the possibility of a presynaptic contributor to quantal size, though the site of Rab3a action (pre- or postsynaptic) cannot be determined without compartment-specific deletion experiments.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'mechanisms observed at a completely different type of synapses cannot be used as an argument for conclusions here' and that 'it is the conclusive data, rather than interpretations that lack concrete evidence, that support ideas and models.' Reviewer 3 notes 'it remains difficult to distinguish if the apparent difference in imaging and electrophysiology is a methodological issue rather than a biological one. Stronger data, especially positive data on changes in release, will be necessary to conclude that pre-synaptic factors are required for HSP.'
